node src/cli.ts edit lp-rubric --body "A rubric is the loop's stop condition, written down as a file in the project it judges. Each project gets two: \`prototype.md\` and \`production.md\`. They are drafted from the repo, the CI workflow and package.json, corrected once, and then the loop runs without further input. The rubric is the only recurring input the loop needs from a person.

Each file has three sections, and the split is not cosmetic. **checks** are deterministic — a command, an exit code, no model involved (#lp-two). **judgements** are graded by an agent, because no exit code answers them. **held-out** is not shown to the builder, and runs once at the end (#lp-split).

## production.md — werk's own, as it would stand today

    checks                          deterministic, exit code decides
      bun test
      bun test --coverage           90% lines on fold.ts, log.ts,
                                    permission.ts, types.ts (#werk-test-scope:src0)
      bun run e2e                   playwright, real server (#werk-test-visual)
      tsc --noEmit

    judgements                      an agent grades each 1-5, 3 to pass
      every acceptance criterion has a test that fails without the change
      each I/O module touched still meets its named behaviour list
      no new exported function in src/ without a doc comment naming its card
      no code path rewrites or deletes a line of .werk/log.jsonl
      card text is never mutated outside the CLI (#werk-write)

    held-out                        the coordinator runs this after the merge.
                                    Builders never see this file.
      boot the server on a copy of log.jsonl, open a card, post a note,
        assert it lands in the log and re-renders
      run add -> link -> status decided -> reopen -> rederive in sequence,
        assert the derived stale set matches a hand-computed one
      the pure-module coverage number, measured against tests written by
        the held-out author, not by the builder

Three of the five judgements are project rules that no generic linter knows. That is what a rubric is for. The two coverage-shaped lines are checks, not judgements, because a number decides them.

The held-out block tests **composition** — server plus log plus fold plus browser in one path — not isolated features. #lp-split gives the reason: a builder optimises whatever it can see, and features it can see in isolation are the cheapest thing to fake.

## prototype.md — werk's own

    checks
      the artifact exists at the declared path
      its entry point exits 0, if it has one

    judgements
      the artifact answers the question the fork asked, and nothing more
      where the brief was silent, the reading it chose is stated in one line
      nothing was written outside the worktree or scratch dir (#al-ephem)

    not checked, on purpose
      coverage, lint, doc comments, naming, dead code, commit hygiene

The 'not checked' block is the part that makes a prototype rubric worth writing. Without it a builder applies production habits to a throwaway and the prototype stops being cheap."

A rubric is the loop's stop condition as a file in the repo. Two per project: `prototype.md` and `production.md`. Both examples are now on #lp-rubric, written for werk itself.

Three sections, and the split is the whole point:

```
checks        deterministic — a command and an exit code, no model
judgements    an agent grades each 1-5, 3 to pass
held-out      the coordinator runs it after the merge; builders never see it
```

werk's `production.md` checks are `bun test`, `bun test --coverage` at 90% on fold/log/permission/types, `bun run e2e`, `tsc --noEmit`. Its judgements are the part no linter knows:

- every acceptance criterion has a test that fails without the change
- no code path rewrites or deletes a line of `.werk/log.jsonl`
- card text is never mutated outside the CLI

Note where the line falls. The coverage number is a **check**, not a judgement, because a number decides it. "Does each I/O module still meet its behaviour list" is a judgement, because #werk-test-scope rule 3 forbids a percentage there.

The held-out block tests composition — server plus log plus fold plus browser in one path — not isolated features. #lp-split's reason: a builder optimises what it can see, and isolated features are the cheapest thing to fake.

`prototype.md` is mostly the inverse, and its best section is the last one:

```
not checked, on purpose
  coverage, lint, doc comments, naming, dead code, commit hygiene
```

Without that block a builder applies production habits to a throwaway, and the prototype stops being cheap.

I also rewrote the card's why — it had read "You answered this one instantly", which is the session-state wording you cut on #werk-loop.

Next: #lp-rubric is still open and its only recorded alternatives are about *when* rubrics are written, not what is in them. Tell me if the two files above are close enough to decide it.

node src/cli.ts edit werk-loop-done --why "The inner loop stops when the production rubric's checks pass. A retry cap decides what happens when they do not." --body "One pass over one ticket ends in one of three states: the checks pass, the checks fail and a retry remains, or the cap is reached.

The checks are #lp-rubric's \`production\` block, not a new list:

    bun test
    bun test --coverage      90% on fold.ts, log.ts, permission.ts, types.ts
    bun run e2e
    tsc --noEmit

On a fail, the next pass is a fresh agent with the same brief plus the last failure, per #lp-stateless. Nothing else carries over.

On the cap, stop the run and leave the branch where it is. Do not move to the next ticket with a broken tree underneath it — a second ticket built on a red base makes the failure harder to attribute, not easier.

**What a builder pass does not run.** The \`judgements\` block and the \`held-out\` block of the same rubric. Judgements need a grader agent, which is #lp-two, still open. Held-out is withheld from the builder by definition and belongs to #werk-loop-merge, which runs after the merge on a tree no single builder controls.

So the builder's bar is exit codes only. The graded and held-out bars exist and are placed; they are just not this pass's job.

Open: the retry number."

**#lp-rubric is decided** — retitled "Two rubrics, prototype and production, built into the tool".

Two constants werk ships with. The loop picks by what happens to the output: `prototype` when the artifact is thrown away, `production` when the code is merged. Both bodies are on the card, with checks / judgements / held-out kept separate.

The per-project-file version is recorded as **#lp-rubric:opt3**, deferred rather than rejected — it is what these become once a second project exists. Also on the card, so it does not surprise anyone later: the production checks name `bun`, `tsc` and playwright, and the judgements name `.werk/log.jsonl` and the werk CLI. Pointing the loop at a second project means editing werk's source. That is the trigger for opt3.

Two knock-ons I applied:

**#werk-loop-done** no longer says "no rubric". Its checks are now the production block by reference, not a duplicate list. A builder pass runs exit codes only — the `judgements` block needs a grader (#lp-two, still open) and `held-out` is withheld from builders by definition.

**#werk-loop-merge** is where held-out runs: different agent, after the merge, on a tree no single builder controls. That closes the reward-hacking hole v0 had accepted, for one extra test command.

One card now out of date: **#lp-split** carries a stale mark from 2026-09-01 and its text predates the held-out block existing. I left a note rather than rewriting it.

Next: re-derive #lp-split against the new #lp-rubric, or rule on #werk-loop-done's open retry number.
